newsitem.title: UK: All eyes on UK's SFO ahead of next move in MGAM probe.
newsitem.headline: All eyes on UK's SFO ahead of next move in MGAM probe.

text.p: Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) said on Friday it was keeping close tabs on the inquiry into three Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) funds but would not confirm reports it was about to launch its own probe.

"We continue, as we have done, to monitor events," an SFO spokesman said. The office is widely expected to take on the investigation, which is currently being conducted by investments watchdog IMRO and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Banking sources said the SFO, which investigates and prosecutes major financial crimes, is now likely to make its move early next week. It has been watching since irregularities were first exposed in the funds nearly four weeks ago.

Last week MGAM sacked fund manager Peter Young on grounds of alleged "gross misconduct". Two of the funds he managed were temporarily suspended when "suspected irregularities" were unearthed but began trading again after a cash bail-out by Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's parent Deutsche Bank.

The bank stepped in to take on unlisted stocks whose valuations were under question. Following investor withdrawals once trading in the funds resumed, Deutsche said it would support the funds for at least three months.

Young, 38, could not be reached by telephone but two weeks ago was reported as saying he was being made a scapegoat. His lawyers, Peters & Peters have said there were no grounds for allegations of criminality against him.

The SFO has been in the spotlight since last Thursday when its decision to press ahead with a second trial in the Maxwell affair, following the acquittal of Ian and Kevin Maxwell in January after an eight-month trial, was overturned by a judge.

Fraud experts said while last week's ruling raised the temperature of the debate over whether juries should be used in complex fraud cases, it would have no impact on whether the SFO decided to take on the MGAM case.
If there was fraud involved, the SFO would become involved as soon as it was convinced an inquiry was needed, one said.

"They have to take such cases on. There's not an option on that. But there's no reason why the Morgan Grenfell investigation should be anything like the complexity of the Maxwell one. It appears to have been over a limted time and in a specific area," said a fraud expert at one major firm.
Suggestions that the SFO was holding back from acting in the MGAM affair as a result of the Maxwell ruling or that morale had been hit were unfounded, he added.

The SFO strongly denied morale at its Elm Street headquarters in central London had been knocked by the decision not to allow a second trial of Kevin Maxwell, son of media baron Robert Maxwell who drowned in 1991.
"Morale is very good at the SFO. We've got our highest ever case load and our officers are getting on with what they are paid to do," the SFO spokesman said.

This had been the case for the last 18 months since uncertainty over the fraud office's future was lifted when the government accepted the recommendations of a report backing the role of the fraud investigators, he added.
